newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb protesters set car parade to beat march ban.
newsitem.headline: Serb protesters set car parade to beat march ban.

text.p: Serbian opposition protesters plan to bring Belgrade to a standstill on Sunday with a slow-motion cavalcade of cars to outfox police who have banned street marches.

The Socialist (SPS) government of autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic has faced almost seven straight weeks of demonstrations for having annulled municipal elections won by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition.

Up to 250,000 people have demonstrated daily in cities across Serbia. But police banned street marches after a December 24 riot between Zajedno backers and government loyalists, ostensibly to ease traffic snarl-ups.
Opposition leaders urged their faithful to parade their vehicles at snail's pace through central Belgrade on Sunday afternoon to circumvent police cordons and defy the authorities.

"Drive very slowly -- 5 kmh (3 mph). Our intent is to mount a protest drive along those streets that our president will not allow us to march on," Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno leader, told a throng of 60,000 on the 48th straight day of rallies.

OSCE investigators invited in by Milosevic concluded that Zajedno's claim of fraud was correct and called for reinstatement of the election outcome in 15 disputed cities including the capital Belgrade.

After 10 days of silence, the government on Friday admitted Zajedno had won a few of the smaller cities but contended that in other districts no party gained a majority or the results remained inconclusive pending further study.
The reply, conveyed in a letter to the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, had been designed to ease international pressure on Milosevic.
But diplomats said the response was so limited and murky that it effectively rebuffed the OSCE team's findings.
The United States weighed in to denounce the SPS's "hollow assurances" of commitment to democratic principles.

Western governments led by Washington have told Milosevic to forget about financial aid to rebuild the disintegrating economy of Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia unless Zajedno's victories are reinstated and broad democratic reforms undertaken.
Zajedno denounced the SPS' answer to the OSCE as a pack of lies and vowed a marathon campaign of protests until all its electoral victories were honoured.
The SPS cited unspecified "irregularities" in voiding the election results.
Police have since bottled up Zajedno protesters in squares and pedestrian malls where they cannot snarl traffic.
"We have decided that tomorrow people from all parts of Belgrade will get into cars and drive towards ... streets which have been taken away from you," Draskovic said.
"If you don't have a car, drive a tractor, a bulldozer, a motorcycle, a bus or a bicycle -- anything that can move -- take it out into the streets."
The parade was to last from 2 to 3 p.m. (1300-1400 gmt).
Any changing of the political guard at the municipal level would signal an end to monolithic leftist power dating to 1945.

In a hint of cracks within the SPS, the moderate mayor of Belgrade, Nebojsa Covic, has resigned, independent media reported on Saturday. Covic was supposed to have handed his post over to opposition leader Zoran Djindjic weeks ago.
